definition.text: The law of conservation of energy applied to heat and work: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.

facts.text: In an isolated system, the total of all forms of energy stays constant.
It distinguishes two main ways energy moves into or out of a system: as heat and as work.
It has been precisely supported, and never violated, in many careful experiments.
Kenneth Boulding used the conservation of matter and energy to argue that the flow of resources through the economy roughly measures GNP, so GNP should be treated as a cost to minimise.

title: Heterodox economics

definition.text: A broad term for schools of economic thought that are not generally seen as part of mainstream economics.

facts.text: It is defined by contrast with whichever schools are most influential at a given time and place, so it has no fixed definition.
Schools usually counted as heterodox include the Austrian, ecological, Marxist-historical, post-Keynesian and modern monetary approaches.
Four frames of analysis are central to heterodox thought: history, natural systems, uncertainty and power.
It is an umbrella term rather than a single school, but its schools often see neoclassical economics as flawed.
Economist Marcos Lisboa argues that the assumptions critics attack are often not essential to neoclassical economics.
Frederic S. Lee estimated in 2007 that 5 to 10 percent of American economists were heterodox.
Student movements such as Rethinking Economics campaign for more pluralism, including heterodox approaches, in economics degrees.

contested_note: Heterodox schools reject parts of neoclassical economics, while mainstream defenders say the criticisms misread it.

title: Heterodox critique of homo economicus
article: Heterodox economics#Criticism of the neoclassical model of individual behavior

definition.text: The objection, shared by many heterodox schools, to the neoclassical picture of people as rational agents who maximise their own utility or profit.

facts.text: Rational, maximising behaviour underpins rational choice theory and is for many economists synonymous with economic behaviour.
Critics note that social constraints or coercion, or poor judgement of choices, may stop people from maximising pleasure.
Shiozawa argues agents in a complex world cannot reach maximum utility and instead pick from a repertoire of ready-made rules.

contested_note: Heterodox and neoclassical economists disagree over whether rational maximisation describes real behaviour.

title: Heterodox critique of market equilibrium
article: Heterodox economics#Criticism of the neoclassical model of market equilibrium

definition.text: The objection that neoclassical models of markets settling at efficient equilibrium prices rarely capture real markets.

facts.text: In microeconomic theory, many cost-minimising buyers and sellers imply market-clearing equilibrium prices, which are Pareto efficient under convexity assumptions.
Mainstream microeconomics is built on optimisation and equilibrium, while heterodox economics centres on institutions, history and social structure.

contested_note: Austrians, post-Keynesians and others dispute the realism of equilibrium models that mainstream economics relies on.
